title: Hall's theorem for solvable groups (converse of Lagrange)

problemStatement.formal: IsHallSubgroup(H) := Nat.Coprime |H| (|G|/|H|); for finite solvable groups, Hall divisors have Hall subgroups and Hall subgroups of the same order are conjugate, while A_4 shows divisibility alone does not imply subgroup existence.
problemStatement.plain: Formalizes Hall's theorem (1928) — the partial converse of Lagrange's theorem for solvable groups. A Hall subgroup has order coprime to its index; Hall's theorem states every Hall divisor of a solvable group's order yields a subgroup, and all such subgroups are conjugate. Proves Hall subgroup properties, Sylow-Hall relationship, index-2 Hall criterion, coprimality infrastructure, the A₄ counterexample (6|12 but no subgroup of order 6), and normal Hall uniqueness.
whyMatters: Hall's theorem is the solvable-group partial converse to Lagrange's theorem.
The A4 counterexample keeps the entry honest about why a full converse to Lagrange fails.
The formalization connects Sylow theory, coprime-index subgroups, and normal Hall complement facts.
